Hierarchies of Manakov–Santini Type
by Means of Rota–Baxter and Other Identities

Błażej M. SZABLIKOWSKI
Abstract

The Lax–Sato approach to the hierarchies of Manakov–Santini type is formalized in order to extend it to a more general class of integrable systems. For this purpose some linear operators are introduced, which must satisfy some integrability conditions, one of them is the Rota–Baxter identity. The theory is illustrated by means of the algebra of Laurent series, the related hierarchies are classified and examples, also new, of Manakov–Santini type systems are constructed, including those that are related to the dispersionless modified Kadomtsev–Petviashvili equation and so called dispersionless rr-th systems.

keywords
Manakov–Santini hierarchy; Rota–Baxter identity; classical rr-matrix formalism; generalized Lax hierarchies; integrable (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional systems

1 Introduction

In recent years, one of the significant achievements in the theory of integrable systems was the construction of formal solutions of the Cauchy problems for a wide class of (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional dispersionless systems by means of the inverse scattering transform [14, 15, 16, 17, 18]. In this process one of the crucial steps was the introduction by Manakov and Santini of a two-field system that generalizes the dispersionless Kadomtsev–Petviashvili (KP) equation. The Manakov–Santini system possesses a non-Hamiltonian Lax pair and the construction of related hierarchy [15] within the Lax–Sato formalism [6, 8] unifies two original approaches based on different underlying structures: first by Takasaki and Takebe [33, 34] and the second one by Martínez Alonso and Shabat [21, 22, 23]. The Manakov–Santini hierarchy and its generalizations were further studied in several works, see for instance [6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 25].

The aim of this work is an extension of the Lax–Sato formalism of Manakov–Santini hierarchy to a more general class of integrable systems, in particular such as the dispersionless modified KP equation or the so-called rr-th systems [2, 3, 4]. Influenced by the papers [7, 8, 9, 10] we generalize the Lax–Sato formalism of Manakov–Santini hierarchy by means of the Lax hierarchy (2.1), where two linear operators 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are introduced. In Theorem 2.3 we find the conditions, on the operators 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R}, for the mutual commutativity of equations from the hierarchy (2.1). One of the conditions turns out to be the well-known Rota–Baxter identity [1, 26, 27]. The general source of the relations in Theorem 2.3 is explained in Section 3. In fact, these relations are directly connected with those that are used in the work [31] for the construction of Frobenius manifolds in the cotangent bundles. In Section 4 we illustrate the above construction by means of the algebra of Laurent series. The related hierarchies (2.1) are classified and there are presented examples of integrable systems of Manakov–Santini type, including new ones.

2 Generalized hierarchy

Let 𝔸\mathbb{A} be a commutative associative unital algebra11 1 We assume, for simplicity, that all structures in this work are defined over the field of complex numbers.. We define the generalized Lax hierarchy of evolution equations by

Ψtn=An​Ψx−Bn​∂Ψ,Ψ=(LM),n∈ℕ,\displaystyle\Psi_{t_{n}}=A_{n}\Psi_{x}-B_{n}\partial\Psi,\qquad\Psi=\begin{pmatrix}L\\ M\end{pmatrix},\qquad n\in\mathbb{N}, (2.1)

where L,M∈𝔸L,M\in\mathbb{A} are Lax and Orlov operators (functions), respectively. The independent variables are evolution parameters (times) tnt_{n} and the spatial variable xx. We assume that ∂\partial is some (auxiliary) derivation in the algebra 𝔸\mathbb{A} invariant with respect to all tnt_{n} and xx. The hierarchy is generated by the functions

An:=𝒫⁡(J−1​∂Xn)andBn:=ℛ⁡(J−1​(Xn)x),Xn:=Ln,\displaystyle A_{n}:=\mathcal{P}\bigl(J^{-1}\partial X_{n}\bigr)\qquad\text{and}\qquad B_{n}:=\mathcal{R}\bigl(J^{-1}(X_{n})_{x}\bigr),\qquad X_{n}:=L^{n}, (2.2)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are some linear maps 𝔸→𝔸\mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{A} and

J:={L,M}≡∂L​Mx−Lx​∂M.\displaystyle J:=\{L,M\}\equiv\partial LM_{x}-L_{x}\partial M. (2.3)

We assume that the endomorphisms 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R} are invariant with respect to times tnt_{n} and the spatial variable xx, that is 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R} commute with derivatives related to tnt_{n} and xx.

In all the following proofs we will skip most of straightforward computations, however we will exhibit all the crucial intermediate steps.

Proposition 2.1.

The evolution equations from the hierarchy (2.1) pairwise commute if the following pair of zero-curvature type equations is satisfied by the generating functions AnA_{n} and BnB_{n}:

(An)tm−(Am)tn+⟨An,Am⟩x+Bm​∂An−Bn​∂Am=0\displaystyle(A_{n})_{t_{m}}-(A_{m})_{t_{n}}+\langle A_{n},A_{m}\rangle_{x}+B_{m}\partial A_{n}-B_{n}\partial A_{m}=0 (2.4a)

and

(Bn)tm−(Bm)tn+An​(Bm)x−Am​(Bn)x−⟨Bn,Bm⟩∂=0,\displaystyle(B_{n})_{t_{m}}-(B_{m})_{t_{n}}+A_{n}(B_{m})_{x}-A_{m}(B_{n})_{x}-\langle B_{n},B_{m}\rangle_{\partial}=0, (2.4b)

where

⟨a,b⟩x:=a​bx−b​ax,⟨a,b⟩∂:=a​∂b−b​∂a.\displaystyle\langle a,b\rangle_{x}:=ab_{x}-ba_{x},\qquad\langle a,b\rangle_{\partial}:=a\partial b-b\partial a.
Proof 2.2.

The commuting of the respective flows means that (Ψtn)tm=(Ψtm)tn(\Psi_{t_{n}})_{t_{m}}=(\Psi_{t_{m}})_{t_{n}}. Comparing the coefficients of both sides with respect to the independent variables Ψx\Psi_{x} and ∂Ψ\partial\Psi we obtain the required pair of zero-curvature conditions.

Theorem 2.3.

The following set of conditions on the endomorphisms 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R}:

𝒫⁡(𝒫⁡(a)​b+a​𝒫​(b))−𝒫⁡(a)​𝒫​(b)=κ1​𝒫​(a​b),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(a)b+a\mathcal{P}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{P}(a)\mathcal{P}(b)=\kappa_{1}\mathcal{P}(ab), (2.5a)
𝒫⁡(ℛ⁡(a)​∂b+a​∂𝒫⁡(b))−ℛ⁡(a)​∂𝒫⁡(b)=κ1​𝒫​(a​∂b),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a)\partial b+a\partial\mathcal{P}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{R}(a)\partial\mathcal{P}(b)=\kappa_{1}\mathcal{P}(a\partial b), (2.5b)
ℛ⁡(𝒫⁡(a)​b+a​ℛ​(b))−𝒫⁡(a)​ℛ​(b)=κ2​ℛ​(a​b),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(a)b+a\mathcal{R}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{P}(a)\mathcal{R}(b)=\kappa_{2}\mathcal{R}(ab), (2.5c)
ℛ⁡(ℛ⁡(a)​∂b+a​∂ℛ⁡(b))−ℛ⁡(a)​∂ℛ⁡(b)=κ2​ℛ​(a​∂b),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a)\partial b+a\partial\mathcal{R}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{R}(a)\partial\mathcal{R}(b)=\kappa_{2}\mathcal{R}(a\partial b), (2.5d)

where a,b∈𝔸a,b\in\mathbb{A} and κ1,κ2∈ℂ\kappa_{1},\kappa_{2}\in\mathbb{C}, is sufficient for the zero-curvature equations (2.4) to be identically fulfilled by the generating functions AnA_{n} and BnB_{n}. This means that the above equations are sufficient conditions for mutual commutation of the flows from the hierarchy (2.1).

Proof 2.4.

Let’s define

an:=J−1​∂Xnandbn:=J−1​(Xn)x,\displaystyle a_{n}:=J^{-1}\partial X_{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad b_{n}:=J^{-1}(X_{n})_{x},

so that An=𝒫⁡(an)A_{n}=\mathcal{P}(a_{n}) and Bn=ℛ⁡(bn)B_{n}=\mathcal{R}(b_{n}). Using (2.1) one finds that

(Xn)tm=Am​(Xn)x−Bm​∂Xn\displaystyle(X_{n})_{t_{m}}=A_{m}(X_{n})_{x}-B_{m}\partial X_{n}

and

Jtn=(An​J)x−∂(Bn​J)⇒(J−1)tn=⟨An,J−1⟩x−⟨Bn,J−1⟩∂.\displaystyle J_{t_{n}}=(A_{n}J)_{x}-\partial(B_{n}J)\quad\Rightarrow\quad\big(J^{-1}\big)_{t_{n}}=\langle A_{n},J^{-1}\rangle_{x}-\langle B_{n},J^{-1}\rangle_{\partial}.

Hence,

(an)tm=⟨Am,an⟩x+bn​∂Am−Bm​∂an,(bn)tm=Am​(bn)x−an​(Bm)x−⟨Bm,bn⟩∂.\displaystyle(a_{n})_{t_{m}}=\langle A_{m},a_{n}\rangle_{x}+b_{n}\partial A_{m}-B_{m}\partial a_{n},\qquad(b_{n})_{t_{m}}=A_{m}(b_{n})_{x}-a_{n}(B_{m})_{x}-\langle B_{m},b_{n}\rangle_{\partial}.

Now substituting (An)tm≡ℛ⁡((an)tm)(A_{n})_{t_{m}}\equiv\mathcal{R}((a_{n})_{t_{m}}) and (Bn)tm≡ℛ⁡((an)tm)(B_{n})_{t_{m}}\equiv\mathcal{R}((a_{n})_{t_{m}}) into the pair of zero-curvature equations (2.4) and taking advantage of the relations (2.5) one finds that

(An)tm+An​(Am)x+Bm​∂An−n↔m\displaystyle(A_{n})_{t_{m}}+A_{n}(A_{m})_{x}+B_{m}\partial A_{n}-n\leftrightarrow m
=𝒫⁡(Am​(an)x+am​(An)x)−Am​(An)x−𝒫⁡(Bm​∂an+bm​∂An)+Bm​∂An−n↔m\displaystyle\qquad{}=\mathcal{P}\bigl(A_{m}(a_{n})_{x}+a_{m}(A_{n})_{x}\bigr)-A_{m}(A_{n})_{x}-\mathcal{P}\bigl(B_{m}\partial a_{n}+b_{m}\partial A_{n}\bigr)+B_{m}\partial A_{n}-n\leftrightarrow m
=κ1​𝒫​(am​(an)x−an​(am)x−bm​∂an+bn​∂am)\displaystyle\qquad{}=\kappa_{1}\mathcal{P}\bigl(a_{m}(a_{n})_{x}-a_{n}(a_{m})_{x}-b_{m}\partial a_{n}+b_{n}\partial a_{m}\bigr)
=κ1​𝒫​(J−1​∂(J−1​{Xm,Xn}))=0\displaystyle\qquad{}=\kappa_{1}\mathcal{P}\bigl(J^{-1}\partial(J^{-1}\{X_{m},X_{n}\})\bigr)=0

and

(Bn)tm−Am​(Bn)x−Bn​∂Bm−n↔m\displaystyle(B_{n})_{t_{m}}-A_{m}(B_{n})_{x}-B_{n}\partial B_{m}-n\leftrightarrow m
=ℛ⁡(Am​(bn)x+am​(Bn)x)−Am​(Bn)x−ℛ⁡(Bm​∂bn+bm​∂Bn)+Bm​∂Bn−n↔m\displaystyle\qquad{}=\mathcal{R}\bigl(A_{m}(b_{n})_{x}+a_{m}(B_{n})_{x}\bigr)-A_{m}(B_{n})_{x}-\mathcal{R}\bigl(B_{m}\partial b_{n}+b_{m}\partial B_{n}\bigr)+B_{m}\partial B_{n}-n\leftrightarrow m
=κ2​ℛ​(am​(bn)x−an​(bm)x−bm​∂bn+bn​∂bm)\displaystyle\qquad{}=\kappa_{2}\mathcal{R}\bigl(a_{m}(b_{n})_{x}-a_{n}(b_{m})_{x}-b_{m}\partial b_{n}+b_{n}\partial b_{m}\bigr)
=κ2​ℛ​(J−1​(J−1​{Xm,Xn})x)=0.\displaystyle\qquad{}=\kappa_{2}\mathcal{R}\bigl(J^{-1}(J^{-1}\{X_{m},X_{n}\})_{x}\bigr)=0.

In the above n↔mn\leftrightarrow m stands for all the remaining terms arising from the permutation of the indices mm and nn in the preceding terms. Since {Xm,Xn}=0\{X_{m},X_{n}\}=0 we see that the zero-curvature equations (2.4) are indeed satisfied identically.

Lemma 2.5.

Assume that the endomorphisms 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℛ\mathcal{R} satisfy the following relation

𝒫⁡(∂a)=∂ℛ⁡(a)\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\partial a)=\partial\mathcal{R}(a) (2.6)

for arbitrary a∈𝔸a\in\mathbb{A}. Then, under the constraint

J≡{L,M}=Ls,\displaystyle J\equiv\{L,M\}=L^{s}, (2.7)

where ss is some fixed integer, the generalized hierarchy (2.1) reduces to the standard hierarchy of the form

Ltn=nn−s​{ℛ⁡(Ln−s),L},\displaystyle L_{t_{n}}=\frac{n}{n-s}\{\mathcal{R}(L^{n-s}),L\}, (2.8)

where the Poisson bracket is defined through the formula (2.3), that is {,}:=∂∧∂x\{,\}:=\partial\wedge\partial_{x}.

On the other hand, if we assume that LL is invariant with respect to times tnt_{n} and the variable xx, that is Ltn=Lx=0L_{t_{n}}=L_{x}=0, then the hierarchy reduces to

Mtn=n​𝒫​(Mx−1​Ln−1)​Mx.\displaystyle M_{t_{n}}=n\mathcal{P}\bigl(M_{x}^{-1}L^{n-1}\bigr)M_{x}. (2.9)
Proof 2.6.

Taking advantage of the constraint (2.7) and the relation (2.6) we have

An=𝒫⁡(J−1​∂Xn)=nn−r​𝒫​(∂Ln−r)=nn−r​∂ℛ⁡(Ln−r)\displaystyle A_{n}=\mathcal{P}\bigl(J^{-1}\partial X_{n}\bigr)=\frac{n}{n-r}\mathcal{P}\bigl(\partial L^{n-r}\bigr)=\frac{n}{n-r}\partial\mathcal{R}(L^{n-r})

and

Bn=ℛ⁡(J−1​(Xn)x)=nn−r​ℛ​((Ln−r)x)=nn−r​(ℛ⁡(Ln−r))x.\displaystyle B_{n}=\mathcal{R}\bigl(J^{-1}(X_{n})_{x}\bigr)=\frac{n}{n-r}\mathcal{R}\bigl((L^{n-r})_{x}\bigr)=\frac{n}{n-r}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(L^{n-r})\bigr)_{x}.

The last relation follows from the assumption that ℛ\mathcal{R} commutes with ∂x\partial_{x}. As result the hierarchy (2.1) reduces into

Ψtn=nn−r​[∂ℛ⁡(Ln−r)​Ψx−(ℛ⁡(Ln−r))x​∂Ψ]≡nn−r​{ℛ⁡(Ln−r),Ψ},\displaystyle\Psi_{t_{n}}=\frac{n}{n-r}\bigl[\partial\mathcal{R}(L^{n-r})\Psi_{x}-\bigl(\mathcal{R}(L^{n-r})\bigr)_{x}\partial\Psi\bigr]\equiv\frac{n}{n-r}\{\mathcal{R}(L^{n-r}),\Psi\},

where Ψ=(L,M)T\Psi=(L,M)^{\rm T}. The first equation on LL coincides with (2.8). The second equation gives evolution of MM consistent with the constraint (2.7).

If Ltn=Lx=0L_{t_{n}}=L_{x}=0, then Bn=0B_{n}=0 and J=∂L​MxJ=\partial LM_{x}. Hence

An=𝒫⁡(J−1​∂Xn)=n​𝒫​(Mx−1​Ln−1).\displaystyle A_{n}=\mathcal{P}\bigl(J^{-1}\partial X_{n}\bigr)=n\mathcal{P}\bigl(M_{x}^{-1}L^{n-1}\bigr).

In this case, the first equation in (2.1) for Ψ=L\Psi=L is satisfied identically and the second equation for Ψ=M\Psi=M takes the form (2.9).

3 Rota–Baxter and other identities

Consider some algebra (𝔸,⋅)(\mathbb{A},\cdot). The Rota–Baxter identity [1, 26, 27] for some linear operator 𝒫:𝔸→𝔸\mathcal{P}\colon\mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{A} has the form

𝒫⁡(𝒫⁡(a)⋅b+a⋅𝒫⁡(b))−𝒫⁡(a)⋅𝒫⁡(b)=κ​𝒫​(a⋅b),\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(a)\cdot b+a\cdot\mathcal{P}(b))-\mathcal{P}(a)\cdot\mathcal{P}(b)=\kappa\mathcal{P}(a\cdot b), (3.1)

where a,b,c∈𝔸a,b,c\in\mathbb{A} and κ\kappa is some fixed scalar weight. Alternatively we can write the identity as

ℓ⁡(ℓ⁡(a)⋅b+a⋅ℓ⁡(b))−ℓ⁡(a)⋅ℓ⁡(b)=14​κ2​a⋅b,\displaystyle\ell(\ell(a)\cdot b+a\cdot\ell(b))-\ell(a)\cdot\ell(b)=\frac{1}{4}\kappa^{2}a\cdot b,

where ℓ:=𝒫−12​κ\ell:=\mathcal{P}-\frac{1}{2}\kappa. For an operator 𝒫\mathcal{P} satisfying (3.1) there is always associated operator 𝒫′:=κ−𝒫\mathcal{P}^{\prime}:=\kappa-\mathcal{P}, which satisfies the identity (3.1) for the same weight κ\kappa.

There is a source of simple solutions to the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1). Assume that the algebra 𝔸\mathbb{A} can be decomposed into direct sum of subalgebras, that is

𝔸=𝔸+⊕𝔸−,𝔸±⋅𝔸±⊂𝔸±,𝔸+∩𝔸−={0}.\displaystyle\mathbb{A}=\mathbb{A}_{+}\oplus\mathbb{A}_{-},\qquad\mathbb{A}_{\pm}\cdot\mathbb{A}_{\pm}\subset\mathbb{A}_{\pm},\qquad\mathbb{A}_{+}\cap\mathbb{A}_{-}=\{0\}.

Then, the projections P+P_{+} and P−P_{-} on the subalgebras 𝔸+\mathbb{A}_{+} and 𝔸−\mathbb{A}_{-} satisfy the identity (3.1) for the weight κ=1\kappa=1. Notice that P++P−=1P_{+}+P_{-}=1.

The main feature of the Rota–Baxter identity is that in the case of associative algebra 𝔸\mathbb{A} the identity (3.1) is a sufficient condition for associativity of another multiplication in 𝔸\mathbb{A} given by

a∗𝒫b:=𝒫⁡(a)⋅b+a⋅𝒫⁡(b)−κ​a⋅b≡ℓ⁡(a)⋅b+a⋅ℓ⁡(b).\displaystyle a*_{\mathcal{P}}b:=\mathcal{P}(a)\cdot b+a\cdot\mathcal{P}(b)-\kappa a\cdot b\equiv\ell(a)\cdot b+a\cdot\ell(b).

For more information on the Rota–Baxter algebras see [12, 13].

The special case of the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1), for a Lie algebra (𝔸,[⋅,⋅])(\mathbb{A},[\cdot,\cdot]), is the modified Yang–Baxter equation

ℛ⁡([ℛ⁡(a),b]+[a,ℛ⁡(b)])−[ℛ⁡(a),ℛ⁡(b)]=κ​ℛ​([a,b]).\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl([\mathcal{R}(a),b]+[a,\mathcal{R}(b)]\bigr)-[\mathcal{R}(a),\mathcal{R}(b)]=\kappa\mathcal{R}\bigl([a,b]\bigr). (3.2)

The equation (3.2) is a sufficient condition for the bracket

[a,b]ℛ:=[ℛ⁡(a),b]+[a,ℛ⁡(b)]−κ⁡[a,b]\displaystyle[a,b]_{\mathcal{R}}:=[\mathcal{R}(a),b]+[a,\mathcal{R}(b)]-\kappa[a,b]

to define second Lie bracket in 𝔸\mathbb{A}, in this case the linear map RR is called the classical rr-matrix. The more standard convention is to consider the endomorphism r:=ℛ−12​κr:=\mathcal{R}-\frac{1}{2}\kappa instead of ℛ\mathcal{R}. The classical rr-matrix formalism [28, 29] is known to be very useful in the construction of very broad classes of integrable systems, see also the survey [5] and references therein.

Let’s now consider commutative and associative algebra (𝔸,⋅)(\mathbb{A},\cdot). We define Poisson bracket in 𝔸\mathbb{A} be means of two commuting derivations ∂,∂x∈Der𝔸\partial,\partial_{x}\in\Der\mathbb{A}:

{a,b}:=∂a⋅∂xb−∂xa⋅∂b.\displaystyle\{a,b\}:=\partial a\cdot\partial_{x}b-\partial_{x}a\cdot\partial b. (3.3)

Here, the derivation ∂x\partial_{x} is a counterpart of the derivative with respect to a spatial variable xx and the derivation ∂\partial is a counterpart of the derivative with respect to some auxiliary variable. The following identity on the endomorphism ℛ\mathcal{R} turns out to be important:

ℛ⁡(ℛ⁡(a)​∂b)+ℛ⁡(a​∂ℛ⁡(b))−ℛ⁡(a)​∂ℛ⁡(b)=κ​ℛ​(a​∂b),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a)\partial b\bigr)+\mathcal{R}\bigl(a\partial\mathcal{R}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{R}(a)\partial\mathcal{R}(b)=\kappa\mathcal{R}(a\partial b), (3.4)

where κ\kappa is some constant. Analogically as before, R′=κ−RR^{\prime}=\kappa-R solves (3.4) for the same weight κ\kappa.

Proposition 3.1.

Let us assume that the endomorphism ℛ\mathcal{R} commutes with the derivation ∂x\partial_{x}, that is ℛ∂x=∂xℛ\mathcal{R}\partial_{x}=\partial_{x}\mathcal{R}. Then, the identity (3.4) is a sufficient condition for ℛ\mathcal{R} to satisfy the modified Yang–Baxter equation

ℛ⁡({ℛ⁡(a),b}+{a,ℛ⁡(b)})−{ℛ⁡(a),ℛ⁡(b)}=κ​ℛ​({a,b}),\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl(\{\mathcal{R}(a),b\}+\{a,\mathcal{R}(b)\}\bigr)-\{\mathcal{R}(a),\mathcal{R}(b)\}=\kappa\mathcal{R}\bigl(\{a,b\}\bigr), (3.5)

and so to be a classical rr-matrix for ℛ\mathcal{R} with respect to the Poisson bracket (3.3). This means that

{a,b}ℛ:={ℛ⁡(a),b}+{a,ℛ⁡(b)}−κ⁡{a,b}\displaystyle\{a,b\}_{\mathcal{R}}:=\{\mathcal{R}(a),b\}+\{a,\mathcal{R}(b)\}-\kappa\{a,b\}

is a Lie bracket when the relation (3.4) holds.

The proof is straightforward expanding the formula (3.4) by means of (3.3). In fact, when ℛ\mathcal{R} also commutes with the derivation ∂\partial, the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) is sufficient for ℛ\mathcal{R} to solve the equation (3.4). However, in general (3.1) is more restrictive than (3.4).

Proposition 3.2.

Assume that, on a commutative associative algebra (𝔸,⋅)(\mathbb{A},\cdot), there exists non-degenerate bilinear product (⋅,⋅)𝔸:𝔸×𝔸→ℂ(\cdot,\cdot)_{\mathbb{A}}\colon\mathbb{A}\times\mathbb{A}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}, such that the Frobenius condition holds:

(a⋅b,c)𝔸=(a,b⋅c)𝔸\displaystyle(a\cdot b,c)_{\mathbb{A}}=(a,b\cdot c)_{\mathbb{A}}

and the product is invariant with respect to the derivation ∂∈Der⁡𝔸\partial\in\Der\mathbb{A}:

(∂a,b)𝔸+(a,∂b)𝔸=0.\displaystyle(\partial a,b)_{\mathbb{A}}+(a,\partial b)_{\mathbb{A}}=0.

Then, the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) is equivalent to the ‘dual’ relation:

ℛ⁡(𝒫⁡(a)​b+a​ℛ​(b))−𝒫⁡(a)​ℛ​(b)=κ​ℛ​(a​b),ℛ:=κ−𝒫∗,\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\bigl(\mathcal{P}(a)b+a\mathcal{R}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{P}(a)\mathcal{R}(b)=\kappa\mathcal{R}(ab),\qquad\mathcal{R}:=\kappa-\mathcal{P}^{*},

where (𝒫∗​a,b)𝔸:=(a,𝒫​b)𝔸(\mathcal{P}^{*}a,b)_{\mathbb{A}}:=(a,\mathcal{P}b)_{\mathbb{A}}.

Let additionally assume that the following relation is valid:

𝒫⁡(∂a)=∂ℛ⁡(a).\displaystyle\mathcal{P}(\partial a)=\partial\mathcal{R}(a). (3.6)

Then, from the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) we obtain the relation (3.4) and

𝒫⁡(ℛ⁡(a)​∂b+a​∂𝒫⁡(b))−ℛ⁡(a)​∂𝒫⁡(b)=κ​𝒫​(a​∂b).\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a)\partial b+a\partial\mathcal{P}(b)\bigr)-\mathcal{R}(a)\partial\mathcal{P}(b)=\kappa\mathcal{P}(a\partial b).

For proof see Proposition 3.3 and Lemma 5.3 in [31]22 2 Notice the misprint in formula (5.9) in [31], there is missing minus sign on the right-hand side of the equality.. In the work [31] it is shown that the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) and the equation (3.4) can be significant in the construction of Frobenius manifolds on cotangent bundles inherent to the integrable systems of hydrodynamic type.

Summarizing, the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) coincides with the condition (2.5a) from Theorem 2.3, the sufficient condition (3.4) on ℛ\mathcal{R} to satisfy the modified Yang–Baxter equation (3.5) coincides with (2.5d), and if the relation (3.6) or (2.6) and some additional natural assumptions are satisfied, then the remaining conditions (2.5b) and (2.5c) hold automatically.

4 Application to the algebra of Laurent series

Consider the algebra of Laurent polynomials 𝔸:=ℂ⁡[p,p−1]\mathbb{A}:=\mathbb{C}[p,p^{-1}], it is commutative and associative. When necessary the algebra 𝔸\mathbb{A} can be extended to the algebra of formal Laurent series at ∞\infty: 𝔸∞:=ℂ⁡((p−1))\mathbb{A}^{\infty}:=\mathbb{C}(\!(p^{-1})\!) or the algebra of formal Laurent series at 00: 𝔸0:=ℂ⁡((p))\mathbb{A}^{0}:=\mathbb{C}(\!(p)\!).

Consider decomposition of 𝔸\mathbb{A} in the form

𝔸=𝔸⩾l⊕𝔸<l,A⩾l:=pl​ℂ​[p],A<l:=pl−1​ℂ​[p−1].\displaystyle\mathbb{A}=\mathbb{A}_{\geqslant l}\oplus\mathbb{A}_{<l},\qquad A_{\geqslant l}:=p^{l}\mathbb{C}[p],\qquad A_{<l}:=p^{l-1}\mathbb{C}\big[p^{-1}\big].

The related projections are defined by

[∑iai​pi]⩾l:=∑i⩾lai​piand[∑iai​pi]<l:=∑i<lai​pi.\displaystyle\left[\sum_{i}a_{i}p^{i}\right]_{\geqslant l}:=\sum_{i\geqslant l}a_{i}p^{i}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left[\sum_{i}a_{i}p^{i}\right]_{<l}:=\sum_{i<l}a_{i}p^{i}.

The subsets 𝔸⩾l\mathbb{A}_{\geqslant l} and 𝔸<l\mathbb{A}_{<l} are subalgebras only for l=0l=0 or l=1l=1. As result, the projections on these subalgebras solve the Rota–Baxter identity (3.1) or (2.5a) with the weight κ=1\kappa=1, that is for

𝒫=[⋅]⩾lor𝒫=[⋅]<lifl=0,1.\displaystyle\mathcal{P}=[\cdot]_{\geqslant l}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathcal{P}=[\cdot]_{<l}\quad\text{if}\quad l=0,1. (4.1)

Remember that [⋅]⩾l+[⋅]<l=1[\cdot]_{\geqslant l}+[\cdot]_{<l}=1.

We will look now for solutions of the identity (3.4), where we take the derivative:

∂:=pr∂p,r∈ℤ.\displaystyle\partial:=p^{r}\partial_{p},\qquad r\in\mathbb{Z}.

Then, projections

ℛ=[⋅]⩾k−rorℛ=[⋅]<k−r\displaystyle\mathcal{R}=[\cdot]_{\geqslant k-r}\qquad\text{or}\qquad\mathcal{R}=[\cdot]_{<k-r} (4.2)

solve the identity (3.4) or (2.5d) with κ=1\kappa=1 if

  1. 1)

    r=0r=0 and k=0k=0;

  2. 2)

    r∈ℤr\in\mathbb{Z} and k=1k=1 or k=2k=2;

  3. 3)

    r=2r=2 and k=3k=3.

Notice that the above solutions coincide with the rr-matrices from [3, 32] with respect to the Poisson bracket defined by

{,}r:=pr∂p∧∂x.\displaystyle\{,\}_{r}:=p^{r}\partial_{p}\wedge\partial_{x}. (4.3)

The first two points are consequence of straightforward verification. To show the third point consider the solutions (4.4a) and let L∈𝔸∞L\in\mathbb{A}^{\infty}. Then, the generating functions (2.2) are

An=[pr​(Ln)p{L,M}r]⩾l=[(Ln)p{L,M}0]⩾l\displaystyle A_{n}=\left[\frac{p^{r}(L^{n})_{p}}{\{L,M\}_{r}}\right]_{\geqslant l}=\left[\frac{(L^{n})_{p}}{\{L,M\}_{0}}\right]_{\geqslant l}

where the Poisson bracket is defined by (4.3). Hence, the related hierarchy (2.1) takes the form (4.5a), since the factors p−rp^{-r} and prp^{r} cancel out. For the solutions (4.4b) and L~∈𝔸0\tilde{L}\in\mathbb{A}^{0} the reasoning is similar. The last point follows from simple verification.

For fixed parameters k,rk,r and ll we can consider the Lax functions LL and L~\tilde{L} to be analytic extensions of some function outside and inside, respectively, unit circle on the complex plane. Thus LL and L~\tilde{L} are defined near ∞\infty and 00, respectively, where they have poles. We can choose these poles to be simple. As result we can consider two families of related hierarchies together and postulate Ψ=(L,M,L~,M~)T\Psi=(L,M,\tilde{L},\tilde{M})^{\rm T} in (4.5). This is, inter alia, consequence of the fact that the solutions (4.4a) and (4.4b) are mutually associated through the decomposition of unity:

1=[⋅]⩾l+[⋅]<l=[⋅]⩾k−r+[⋅]<k−r.\displaystyle 1=[\cdot]_{\geqslant l}+[\cdot]_{<l}=[\cdot]_{\geqslant k-r}+[\cdot]_{<k-r}.

The compatibility equations (2.4) for the hierarchies (4.5) takes the following, independent of rr, form:

(Anλ)tmμ−(Amμ)tnλ+⟨Anλ,Amμ⟩x+Bmμ​(Anλ)p−Bnλ​(Amμ)p=0\displaystyle\bigl(A_{n}^{\lambda}\bigr)_{t_{m}^{\mu}}-\bigl(A_{m}^{\mu}\bigr)_{t_{n}^{\lambda}}+\bigl\langle A_{n}^{\lambda},A_{m}^{\mu}\bigr\rangle_{x}+B_{m}^{\mu}\bigl(A_{n}^{\lambda}\bigr)_{p}-B_{n}^{\lambda}\bigl(A_{m}^{\mu}\bigr)_{p}=0 (4.7a)
and

where m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N}; μ,λ=∞,0\mu,\lambda=\infty,0 and ⟨f,g⟩ξ:=f​gξ−g​fξ\langle f,g\rangle_{\xi}:=fg_{\xi}-gf_{\xi} for ξ=x,p\xi=x,p. The related generating functions are defined as

An∞:=[(Ln)p{L,M}0]⩾l,Bn∞:=[(Ln)x{L,M}0]⩾k,\displaystyle A_{n}^{\infty}:=\left[\frac{(L^{n})_{p}}{\{L,M\}_{0}}\right]_{\geqslant l},\qquad B_{n}^{\infty}:=\left[\frac{(L^{n})_{x}}{\{L,M\}_{0}}\right]_{\geqslant k},

and

An0:=[(L~n)p{L~,M~}0]<l,Bn0:=[(L~n)x{L~,M~}0]<k.\displaystyle A_{n}^{0}:=\left[\frac{(\tilde{L}^{n})_{p}}{\{\tilde{L},\tilde{M}\}_{0}}\right]_{<l},\qquad B_{n}^{0}:=\left[\frac{(\tilde{L}^{n})_{x}}{\{\tilde{L},\tilde{M}\}_{0}}\right]_{<k}.

Notice that if we treat Ψ\Psi as a common eigenfunction, then the pairs of equations from (4.5) give the Lax pairs for the respective systems from (4.7).

Let us consider reductions from Lemma 2.5. First for constraints of the type (2.7) we take

{L,M}r=Lrand{L~,M~}r=L~2−r.\displaystyle\{L,M\}_{r}=L^{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\{\tilde{L},\tilde{M}\}_{r}=\tilde{L}^{2-r}. (4.8)

We assume that they are consistent with respect to the appropriate choice of Lax and Orlov functions, see the forthcoming examples. Then, in accordance with equations (2.7) and (2.8) the hierarchies (4.5) reduce to

Ltn∞=nn−r​{[Ln−r]⩾k−r,L}randL~tn0=nn−2+r​{[L~n+2−r]<k−r,L~}r.\displaystyle L_{t^{\infty}_{n}}=\frac{n}{n-r}\bigl\{[L^{n-r}]_{\geqslant k-r},L\bigr\}_{r}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{L}_{t^{0}_{n}}=\frac{n}{n-2+r}\bigl\{[\tilde{L}^{n+2-r}]_{<k-r},\tilde{L}\bigr\}_{r}.

So we obtain the standard Poisson hierarchies of dispersionless systems, see [3, 32] and references therein. For the next reduction from Lemma 2.5 we postulate that

L=pandL~=p−1.\displaystyle L=p\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{L}=p^{-1}.

Then, the hierarchies (4.5) reduce to

Mtn∞=n​[pn−1​Mx−1]⩾l​MxandM~tn0=n​[p1−n​M~x−1]<l​M~x.\displaystyle M_{t^{\infty}_{n}}=n\bigl[p^{n-1}M_{x}^{-1}\bigr]_{\geqslant l}M_{x}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{M}_{t^{0}_{n}}=n\bigl[p^{1-n}\tilde{M}_{x}^{-1}\bigr]_{<l}\tilde{M}_{x}.

Gtn∞=n​⟨[pn−1​G]⩾l,G⟩xandG~tn0=n​⟨[p1−n​G~x]<l,G~⟩x.\displaystyle G_{t^{\infty}_{n}}=n\bigl\langle\bigl[p^{n-1}G\bigr]_{\geqslant l},G\bigr\rangle_{x}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\tilde{G}_{t^{0}_{n}}=n\bigl\langle\bigl[p^{1-n}\tilde{G}_{x}\bigr]_{<l},\tilde{G}\bigr\rangle_{x}.

These are the universal hierarchies considered in [21, 22, 23].

For appropriate choice of Lax functions and associated Orlov functions the Lax hierarchies (4.5), in principle, yield construction of (1+1)(1+1)-dimensional integrable infinite-field (chain) systems, while the compatibility conditions (4.7) provide finite-field systems that include (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional integrable equations of Manakov–Santini type, which are of our interest. Although it would be fairly easy, we will not consider in this work finite-field reductions of Lax hierarchies (4.5).

4.1 The case of 𝒌=𝒍=𝒓=𝟎\boldsymbol{k=l=r=0}

The Lax function [2, 33, 34] has the form

L=p+u⁡(x)​p−1+u2​(x)​p−2+u3​(x)​p−3+⋯∈𝔸∞\displaystyle L=p+u(x)p^{-1}+u_{2}(x)p^{-2}+u_{3}(x)p^{-3}+\cdots\in\mathbb{A}^{\infty}

and the associated Orlov function [33, 34] is

M=M0+x+v⁡(x)​L−1+v2​(x)​L−2+⋯,\displaystyle M=M_{0}+x+v(x)L^{-1}+v_{2}(x)L^{-2}+\cdots,

where M0M_{0} is the part of MM that explicitly depends on times tn∞t^{\infty}_{n} and commutes with LL, that is {M0,L}0≡0\{M_{0},L\}_{0}\equiv 0. This means that the choice of M0M_{0} does not influence the construction of related systems from (4.7). In this case, consistent Lax hierarchy for L~∈𝔸0\tilde{L}\in\mathbb{A}^{0} does not exist.

Then, we calculate

{L,M}0=1+vx​p−1+((v2)x−u)​p−2+⋯\displaystyle\{L,M\}_{0}=1+v_{x}p^{-1}+\bigl((v_{2})_{x}-u\bigr)p^{-2}+\cdots

and the first generating functions

A1∞=1,\displaystyle A^{\infty}_{1}=1,\qquad A2∞=p−vx,\displaystyle A^{\infty}_{2}=p-v_{x},\qquad A3∞=p2−vx​p+2​u+vx2−(v2)x,\displaystyle A^{\infty}_{3}=p^{2}-v_{x}p+2u+v_{x}^{2}-(v_{2})_{x},
B1∞=0,\displaystyle B^{\infty}_{1}=0,\qquad B2∞=ux,\displaystyle B^{\infty}_{2}=u_{x},\qquad B3∞=ux​p+(u2)x−ux​vx.\displaystyle B^{\infty}_{3}=u_{x}p+(u_{2})_{x}-u_{x}v_{x}.

From the generalized zero-curvature equations (4.7) for n=1n=1, m=2m=2 and λ=μ=∞\lambda=\mu=\infty we get

ut1=ux,vt1=vx,\displaystyle u_{t_{1}}=u_{x},\qquad v_{t_{1}}=v_{x},

where t1≡t1∞t_{1}\equiv t^{\infty}_{1}. For n=1n=1, m=3m=3 we get

(u1)t1=(u1)x,(v2)t1=(v2)x.\displaystyle(u_{1})_{t_{1}}=(u_{1})_{x},\qquad(v_{2})_{t_{1}}=(v_{2})_{x}.

Which in fact means that we can identify the time t1t_{1} with xx. First nontrivial equations are for n=2n=2 and m=3m=3. Let t≡t3t\equiv t_{3} and y≡t2y\equiv t_{2}. Hence, we obtain two compatibility conditions:

(v2)x=u+vy+vx2,(u2)x=uy+ux​vx\displaystyle(v_{2})_{x}=u+v_{y}+v_{x}^{2},\qquad(u_{2})_{x}=u_{y}+u_{x}v_{x}

and the celebrated Manakov–Santini system [15]

vx​t=vy​y+vx​vx​y+u​vx​x−vy​vx​x,ux​t=uy​y+ux2+ux​y​vx+u​ux​x−ux​x​vy.\displaystyle\begin{split}&v_{xt}=v_{yy}+v_{x}v_{xy}+uv_{xx}-v_{y}v_{xx},\\ &u_{xt}=u_{yy}+u_{x}^{2}+u_{xy}v_{x}+uu_{xx}-u_{xx}v_{y}.\end{split} (4.9)

The related Lax pair which follows from (4.5a) is

∂yΨ=[(p−vx)∂x−ux∂p]Ψ,\displaystyle\partial_{y}\Psi=\left[(p-v_{x})\partial_{x}-u_{x}\partial_{p}\right]\Psi,
∂tΨ=[(p2−vxp+u−vy)∂x−(uxp+uy)∂p]Ψ.\displaystyle\partial_{t}\Psi=\left[\bigl(p^{2}-v_{x}p+u-v_{y}\bigr)\partial_{x}-\bigl(u_{x}p+u_{y}\bigr)\partial_{p}\right]\Psi.

ux​t=uy​y+ux2+u​ux​x.\displaystyle u_{xt}=u_{yy}+u_{x}^{2}+uu_{xx}.

vx​t=vy​y+vx​vx​y−vy​vx​x.\displaystyle v_{xt}=v_{yy}+v_{x}v_{xy}-v_{y}v_{xx}.

The Lax and the associated Orlov functions for p→0p\rightarrow 0 are

and

A10=0,\displaystyle A^{0}_{1}=0,\qquad A20=vmx​p−1,\displaystyle A^{0}_{2}=\frac{v}{m_{x}}p^{-1},\qquad A30=v2mx​p−2+2​v​v0​mx−v​(m1)xmx2​p−1,\displaystyle A^{0}_{3}=\frac{v^{2}}{m_{x}}p^{-2}+\frac{2vv_{0}m_{x}-v(m_{1})_{x}}{m_{x}^{2}}p^{-1},
B10=0,\displaystyle B^{0}_{1}=0,\qquad B20=−vxmx,\displaystyle B^{0}_{2}=-\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}},\qquad B30=−v​vxmx​p−1+((m1)xmx2−2​v0mx)​vx−v​(v0)xmx.\displaystyle B^{0}_{3}=-\frac{vv_{x}}{m_{x}}p^{-1}+\left(\frac{(m_{1})_{x}}{m_{x}^{2}}-\frac{2v_{0}}{m_{x}}\right)v_{x}-\frac{v(v_{0})_{x}}{m_{x}}.

From the generalized zero-curvature equations (4.7) for n=2n=2, m=3m=3 and λ=μ=0\lambda=\mu=0 we get the constraints

(v0)x=vz​mxv,((m1)xmx)x=mx​z+vzv​mx,\displaystyle(v_{0})_{x}=\frac{v_{z}m_{x}}{v},\qquad\left(\frac{(m_{1})_{x}}{m_{x}}\right)_{x}=m_{xz}+\frac{v_{z}}{v}m_{x},

where z≡t20z\equiv t^{0}_{2}, and the system

(vmx)τ=−[vmx​∂x−1v​(mxv)z]z,(vxmx)τ=vz​z−[vxmx​∂x−1v​(mxv)z]z,\displaystyle\left(\frac{v}{m_{x}}\right)_{\tau}=-\left[\frac{v}{m_{x}}\partial_{x}^{-1}v\left(\frac{m_{x}}{v}\right)_{z}\right]_{z},\qquad\left(\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\right)_{\tau}=v_{zz}-\left[\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\partial_{x}^{-1}v\left(\frac{m_{x}}{v}\right)_{z}\right]_{z}, (4.12)

where τ≡t30\tau\equiv t^{0}_{3}. The Lax pair for (4.12) is given by

∂τΨ=[vmxp−1∂x+vxmx∂p]Ψ,\displaystyle\partial_{\tau}\Psi=\left[\frac{v}{m_{x}}p^{-1}\partial_{x}+\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\partial_{p}\right]\Psi,
∂zΨ=[(v2mxp−2−vmx∂x−1v(mxv)zp−1)∂x+(v​vxmxp−1+vz−vxmx∂x−1v(mxv)z)∂p]Ψ.\displaystyle\partial_{z}\Psi=\left[\left(\frac{v^{2}}{m_{x}}p^{-2}-\frac{v}{m_{x}}\partial_{x}^{-1}v\left(\frac{m_{x}}{v}\right)_{\!z}p^{-1}\right)\partial_{x}+\left(\frac{vv_{x}}{m_{x}}p^{-1}+v_{z}-\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\partial_{x}^{-1}v\left(\frac{m_{x}}{v}\right)_{\!z}\right)\partial_{p}\right]\Psi.

Consider first reduction given by the condition

{L~,M~}r=L~2−r,r∈ℤ,\displaystyle\{\tilde{L},\tilde{M}\}_{r}=\tilde{L}^{2-r},\qquad r\in\mathbb{Z}, (4.13)

which is consistent since order at 00 of both sides is the same. Thus,

{L~,M~}0=p−r​L~2−r=v2−r​p−2+(2−r)​v1−r​v0​p−1+⋯\displaystyle\{\tilde{L},\tilde{M}\}_{0}=p^{-r}\tilde{L}^{2-r}=v^{2-r}p^{-2}+(2-r)v^{1-r}v_{0}p^{-1}+\cdots

and we obtain the constraint

mx=−v1−r,\displaystyle m_{x}=-v^{1-r},

by means of which (4.12) gives the rr-th dispersionless Harry–Dym equation [2, 4]:

vτ=−v1−r​[vr​∂x−1v−r​vz]z.\displaystyle v_{\tau}=-v^{1-r}\bigl[v^{r}\partial_{x}^{-1}v^{-r}v_{z}\bigr]_{z}.

The second reduction is given by the constraint: L~=p−1\tilde{L}=p^{-1}, from which it follows that v=1v=1 and the system (4.12) reduces to [22, 30]

mx​τ=mx​mz​z−mx​z​mz.\displaystyle m_{x\tau}=m_{x}m_{zz}-m_{xz}m_{z}.

Now, we will consider the mixed case. For λ=∞\lambda=\infty, n=1n=1 and μ=0\mu=0 with m=2m=2 or m=3m=3 in (4.7) we obtain

vt1=vx,mt1=mx,\displaystyle v_{t_{1}}=v_{x},\qquad m_{t_{1}}=m_{x},

which holds automatically as t1≡xt_{1}\equiv x. From the zero-curvature equations (4.7), for λ=∞\lambda=\infty, n=2n=2 and μ=0\mu=0, m=2m=2, we obtain the following compatibility equations

uz=vxmx,wx​z=−v​mx​xmx2\displaystyle u_{z}=\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}},\qquad w_{xz}=-v\frac{m_{xx}}{m_{x}^{2}}

and

(vmx)y=vmx​(ux+wx​x)−wx​(vmx)x,(vxmx)y=(ux​v)xmx−wx​(vxmx)x.\displaystyle\left(\frac{v}{m_{x}}\right)_{y}=\frac{v}{m_{x}}(u_{x}+w_{xx})-w_{x}\left(\frac{v}{m_{x}}\right)_{x},\qquad\left(\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\right)_{y}=\frac{(u_{x}v)_{x}}{m_{x}}-w_{x}\left(\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\right)_{x}.

The above equations can be equivalently rewritten in the following form, for which we have the conditions

ux=(log⁡v)y−(log⁡v)x​mymx,wx=−mymx\displaystyle u_{x}=(\log v)_{y}-(\log v)_{x}\frac{m_{y}}{m_{x}},\qquad w_{x}=-\frac{m_{y}}{m_{x}}

and the system

mx​x​v=mx​my​z−my​mx​z,vx​x=(log⁡v)y​z​mx−(log⁡v)x​z​my,\displaystyle m_{xx}v=m_{x}m_{yz}-m_{y}m_{xz},\qquad v_{xx}=(\log v)_{yz}m_{x}-(\log v)_{xz}m_{y}, (4.14)

which is a system of Manakov–Santini type recently obtained in [7]. The related Lax pair is

∂yΨ=[(p+w)∂x−uxp∂p]Ψ,∂zΨ=[vmxp−1∂x+vxmx∂p]Ψ.\displaystyle\partial_{y}\Psi=\left[(p+w)\partial_{x}-u_{x}p\partial_{p}\right]\Psi,\qquad\partial_{z}\Psi=\left[\frac{v}{m_{x}}p^{-1}\partial_{x}+\frac{v_{x}}{m_{x}}\partial_{p}\right]\Psi.

Consider now the reduction by means of (4.11) and (4.13), that is we have constraints in the form

wx=(r−1)​u,mx=−v1−r,r∈ℤ.\displaystyle w_{x}=(r-1)u,\qquad m_{x}=-v^{1-r},\qquad r\in\mathbb{Z}.

Hence, from (4.14) we obtain the rr-th dispersionless Toda system [4, 19]:

uz+vr−1​vx=0,vy=ux​v+(1−r)​u​vx,\displaystyle u_{z}+v^{r-1}v_{x}=0,\qquad v_{y}=u_{x}v+(1-r)uv_{x},

which for r=1r=1 gives the Boyer–Finley equation being (2+1)(2+1)-dimensional version of dispersionless Toda equation. On the other hand from the reduction: L=pL=p, L~=p−1\tilde{L}=p^{-1} we have the constraints: u=0u=0, v=1v=1, from which we get the equation [22, 24]

mx​x=mx​my​z−my​mx​z.\displaystyle m_{xx}=m_{x}m_{yz}-m_{y}m_{xz}.

The remaining not considered cases from Proposition 4.1 are equivalent to the above examples through the transformation (4.6) or there is no consistent hierarchies for them on the level of equations (4.5).
